item.title: Adachi Museum of Art: The Garden as a Living Painting — Guide
item.description: The Adachi Museum of Art in Yasugi is unique: it is a museum whose most celebrated exhibit is its garden. Founded in 1970 by a local businessman, it pairs a serious collection of modern Japanese painting — above all works by Yokoyama Taikan — with vast, meticulously groomed gardens of raked gravel, moss, clipped pines and a distant borrowed mountain. The genius is in the framing: windows and openings turn the gardens into ‘living paintings’ that change with the light and seasons, and the whole is maintained to such perfection that it has been ranked the best garden in Japan for two decades running.

item.title: Korakuen Garden: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens — Guide
item.description: Korakuen, completed in 1700 for the lord of Okayama, is counted among the three great gardens of Japan alongside Kenrokuen and Kairakuen. What sets it apart is its openness: where most Japanese strolling gardens are dense and enclosed, Korakuen spreads wide lawns, ponds and streams across a river island, giving it a rare feeling of light and space. Paths wind past a working tea plantation and small rice field, teahouses, a grove of plum and cherry, and a hill you can climb for the full view — all composed around the borrowed scenery of Okayama Castle’s black keep rising beyond the garden wall.

item.title: Maruyama Park: Kyoto's Favourite Cherry-Blossom Park — Guide
item.description: Maruyama Park, tucked behind Yasaka Shrine at the foot of the Higashiyama hills, is the most popular public park in Kyoto and its most famous spot for hanami. Laid out in the Meiji era, it is a gentle landscape of ponds, streams, stone lanterns and winding paths, with tea houses and restaurants around its edges. At its heart stands a huge shidarezakura, a weeping cherry tree, which in early April is floodlit after dark and surrounded by revellers and food stalls in one of the city’s great cherry-blossom scenes.

item.title: Ohori Park and Fukuoka Castle Ruins — Guide
item.description: Ohori Park is Fukuoka’s most beloved city park, built around a large pond created from the old moat of Fukuoka Castle. A scenic walking and jogging path circles the water, crossing a chain of small islands linked by stone bridges, with willows, pavilions and cafes along the way — a favourite spot for locals to stroll, relax and watch the sunset. Adjoining the park are the stone walls and ruins of Fukuoka Castle (Maizuru Park), once the largest castle in Kyushu, whose ramparts and turret sites give fine views and burst into cherry blossom in spring.

item.title: Rikugien Garden — Guide
item.description: Rikugien, in Tokyo’s Bunkyo ward, is widely regarded as one of the city’s most beautiful traditional Japanese gardens. Completed in 1702, this Edo-period ‘strolling garden’ was designed to recreate in miniature 88 scenes from classical Japanese and Chinese poetry, laid out around a large central pond with small islands, wooded hills, winding paths, stone bridges and elegant teahouses. A leisurely circuit reveals ever-changing views, and you can pause at a teahouse for matcha and a sweet overlooking the water.

item.title: Sengan-en Garden — Guide
item.description: Sengan-en, on the shore of Kinko Bay just north of Kagoshima city, is one of Japan’s finest traditional gardens and a former villa of the powerful Shimazu clan, who ruled the region for nearly 700 years. Laid out in the seventeenth century, its genius lies in its ‘borrowed scenery’ (shakkei): the garden is designed so that the smoking cone of Sakurajima volcano across the bay becomes its centrepiece ‘mountain’, with the sea as its ‘pond’, creating a breathtaking, grand-scale landscape.

item.title: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden — Guide
item.description: Shinjuku Gyoen is one of Tokyo’s largest and most beautiful gardens, a tranquil green oasis of over 58 hectares set right beside the skyscrapers and bustle of Shinjuku. Originally a feudal lord’s residence and later an imperial garden, it opened to the public after the war. Its special charm lies in combining three distinct landscape styles in one park: a spacious, manicured French formal garden with symmetrical flowerbeds and plane-tree avenues; a wide, rolling English landscape garden of open lawns and mature trees; and a classical Japanese garden with ponds, bridges, islands and a traditional teahouse.

item.title: Shukkeien Garden: A Miniature Landscape in the City — Guide
item.description: Shukkeien, whose name means ‘shrunken-scenery garden’, is a beautiful traditional strolling garden in the middle of Hiroshima, laid out in 1620 for the local lord. As its name suggests, it miniaturises whole landscapes — mountains, valleys, forests and a central pond dotted with islets — into a compact space that unfolds scene by scene as you follow the path around the water. An arched rainbow bridge crosses the pond, tea houses sit among the maples and cherries, and carp fill the water.

item.title: Suizenji Garden — Guide
item.description: Suizenji Jōjuen, a beautiful traditional landscape garden in Kumamoto city, was begun in the seventeenth century by the ruling Hosokawa lords as a tea retreat. Designed as a ‘strolling garden’ around a large pond fed by clear spring water from Mount Aso, its most famous feature is a miniature recreation of the 53 post stations of the old Tōkaidō highway between Kyoto and Edo — including a distinctive grassy conical hill representing Mount Fuji — laid out along the walking path so that a stroll around the pond becomes a symbolic journey.

item.title: Tennoji Park & Keitakuen Garden: Green Heart of the South — Guide
item.description: Tennoji Park spreads beneath the towers of Abeno Harukas, a large and varied green space at the junction of the Tennoji and Shinsekai districts. Its jewel is Keitakuen, a circular strolling garden designed in the early twentieth century around a central pond, once the private garden of the Sumitomo family and a masterpiece of the period. The park also holds Osaka’s zoo, the city art museum and, at its northern edge, a modern lawn plaza lined with cafes and lit in the evening — making it a place equally suited to garden lovers, families and anyone wanting to sit down between sights.

item.title: Yuushien Garden: Peonies and Ginseng on Daikonshima — Guide
item.description: Yuushien is a beautiful Japanese strolling garden on Daikonshima, a volcanic island in Lake Nakaumi near Matsue. It is best known for peonies: the island is a major grower, and the garden displays them year-round, most spectacularly in a winter arrangement of hundreds of blooms floating on the surface of the pond. Around a central pond with waterfalls and stepping stones, the garden also grows Korean ginseng, another local speciality, and glows with azaleas in spring and maples in autumn.

item.title: Kinkaku-ji Guide: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion
item.description: A three-storey pavilion covered in pure gold leaf, mirrored perfectly in the still pond before it, framed by pines and — if you’re lucky — dusted with snow or backed by autumn maples: Kinkaku-ji is the postcard image of Kyoto, and one of the few sights that genuinely lives up to it. The Golden Pavilion shimmers whether under bright sun, soft cloud, or a rare winter snowfall, and the moment you round the path and it appears across the water is unforgettable.
